https://www.techtimes.com/articles/32090.text: South Korea and Singapore lead a ten-nation mobile benchmarking study released this week, outperforming the United States, Germany, and every European market on both the quality of their operating environments and what consumers actually receive — a divergence that traces directly to three policy choices the top-ranked nations made and most of the bottom half did not: mandatory 5G Standalone architecture, spectrum allocated on deployment speed rather than price, and regulatory frameworks that let operators sell differentiated network slicing services. VodafoneThree published the Mobile Market Index on July 16, benchmarking ten countries across two dimensions: Operating Environment (how easy or hard it is to build and run a mobile network) and Consumer and Market Outcomes (the quality of service those networks actually deliver). The index lands as the UK government's Mobile Market Review is accepting evidence on how to reach standalone 5G coverage in all populated areas by 2030 — but its findings cut across every market on the scorecard, and the picture they reveal is a study in how similar inputs produce radically different results depending on what governments choose to regulate. VodafoneThree, the UK operator formed by the May 2025 merger of Vodafone and Three, is the UK's largest mobile network operator and is openly using the index to support its three policy asks from the Mobile Market Review — a lobbying context that ISPreview's Mark Jackson correctly noted reflects the operator's own vested interests. But the comparative framework survives the caveat, because the gaps between countries are independently verifiable and the mechanisms behind them are documented in regulatory filings, Opensignal data, and government strategy documents that the operator did not produce. What the Scorecard Says On Operating Environment, Singapore leads with a score of 0.698, South Korea second at 0.667, the United States third at 0.639, and Norway fourth at 0.634. Germany, Australia, and Hungary sit in the middle. The United Kingdom scores 0.481, France 0.422, and Spain 0.410. Consumer and Market Outcomes reshuffles the order significantly. South Korea leads at 0.747, Singapore second at 0.734, Norway third at 0.702. France climbs from ninth to fourth at 0.632. Germany holds fifth at 0.579. Spain rises to sixth at 0.473. Australia and the United States, both strong on operating environment, slip to seventh and eighth at 0.469 and 0.460. The United Kingdom places ninth at 0.449, and Hungary finishes last at 0.410. The two tables together contain the article's real story. Countries can be ranked well on investment environment and still underperform on consumer outcomes — the United States and Australia are the clearest examples — because geography imposes costs that policy cannot fully offset. Countries can rank poorly on investment environment and still sustain acceptable consumer outcomes for a time — France and Spain — because decades of prior infrastructure investment continue to deliver experience even as the environment for new investment deteriorates. And countries can rank well on both, as Singapore and South Korea do, because deliberate policy decisions accelerated the build-out of the right architecture at the right time. The Asia-Pacific Model: Mandate First, Market Second Singapore's path to first place on operating environment is one of deliberate, sequenced state intervention. In 2020, the Infocomm Media Development Authority chose not to auction 5G spectrum to the highest bidder. Instead, it ran a Call for Proposal, awarding spectrum to operators based on the quality and speed of their deployment plans. The winning operators — Singtel and a StarHub-M1 joint venture — were required to build only 5G Standalone networks from day one, bypassing the Non-Standalone architecture that most Western markets spent years deploying before upgrading. The outcome: Singtel announced nationwide 5G SA outdoor coverage in July 2022, three years ahead of its regulatory target and making Singapore what the US Department of Commerce later described as the first country in the world fully covered by Standalone 5G. By mid-2026, M1 and StarHub had completed their own full 5G SA transitions; operators were actively migrating customers from any remaining NSA infrastructure to SA services. Government R&D investment of SGD 25 billion through 2025 created demand-side pull for 5G applications, meaning operators had enterprise customers ready to buy sliced services the day the network could deliver them. South Korea's route was different in mechanism but identical in outcome. The Ministry of Science and ICT is requiring all 5G base stations to connect to 5G Standalone core equipment in 2026 — a government mandate, not a commercial choice. KT, the first Korean operator to deploy 5G SA in June 2021, is already reporting the fastest 5G download speeds in the country as a result. South Korea's network slicing market is projected to reach $1.72 billion in 2026 as SK Telecom and others expand commercial slicing deployments across smart factories, logistics operations, and smart city infrastructure. Industrial IoT penetration on sliced networks is expected to climb from 25% in 2025 to 48% by 2030. Both countries prove the same point: operator investment follows government signal. When governments make the architecture decision — SA only — and provide regulatory frameworks that allow operators to monetize the resulting capabilities through slicing, the investment case for infrastructure spending closes. When they leave the architecture choice to the market and block the revenue stream, it does not. Norway: Geography as the Hardest Opponent Norway's third-place consumer outcomes score is among the most analytically interesting in the index, because it disproves the easy argument that favorable geography explains top performance. Norway has some of the most challenging terrain for mobile deployment on earth: fjords that block signal propagation, mountain ranges that require expensive site acquisition, a population density of fewer than fifteen people per square kilometer outside of Oslo and Bergen, and an Arctic north where permafrost complicates ground-level infrastructure. Despite all of that, Norway's 5G population coverage reached 99.7% in 2024. Oslo averages approximately 231 Mbps on mobile, Bergen around 187 Mbps — competitive with South Korea's best cities. Telenor won 11 of 15 available categories in Opensignal's November 2025 Norwegian network report. Telia Norway launched 5G SA commercially as 'Avansert 5G' to B2B customers in February 2026; Telenor and Telia simultaneously announced the country's first cross-operator network sharing agreement to extend coverage beyond each network's individual footprint. The Norwegian operating environment is not effortless — the MMI places it fourth, not first — but what it has that the UK, France, and Spain do not is a regulatory framework calibrated around investment sustainability rather than price minimization. Norway's three-operator market has competition but not the margin-crushing price war that defines France's four-operator-plus-MVNO ecosystem. Its energy costs, while rising, are structurally lower than the UK's. And it operates no equivalent of the net neutrality bar on commercial slicing that prevents UK and European operators from monetizing the capabilities their networks can technically deliver. Germany: Good Breadth, Weak Industrial Depth Germany illustrates a different kind of divergence — between headline coverage statistics and the specific technical capability that determines whether 5G is industrially useful. Germany's 5G coverage reached 95% of national territory by October 2025, with Deutsche Telekom providing the widest footprint at approximately 87% geographic coverage, Vodafone and Telefónica each at 75–76%. Telekom's 5G download speeds reached 173.8 Mbps in Opensignal's November 2025 German market report, comfortably ahead of Vodafone at 154.3 Mbps and O2 at 114.5 Mbps. But the EU Digital Decade 2026 progress report identified a structural gap that headline coverage figures conceal: Germany achieves only 54.43% coverage in the 3.4–3.8 GHz spectrum band, which is the frequency range most critical for industrial IoT and enterprise 5G applications because it balances range and data capacity. The EU average for the same band is nearly 75%. Germany's industrial heartland — manufacturing, automotive, chemicals — sits on a 5G network that is wide enough for consumer mobile but thin on the frequencies that make factory automation, machine-to-machine communication, and logistics optimization genuinely viable at scale. Germany's sixth-place operating environment score reflects structural strengths: lower energy costs than the UK, a spectrum licensing regime that ties frequency awards to coverage obligations through the Bundesnetzagentur, and a 5G Standalone rollout that is accelerating. Its fifth-place consumer outcomes score is consistent with those strengths. But the industrial band gap is the number the operating environment score does not capture — and for Germany, which has staked its economic future on manufacturing digitalization, it is the one that matters most. The United States: Scale as the Variable That Won't Bend The United States sits third on operating environment and eighth on consumer outcomes, a gap of five positions that is almost entirely explained by its size. Covering 3.8 million square miles of varied terrain — mountain ranges, plains, forests, and approximately 2 million square miles of territory with population densities under one person per square mile — at comparable quality to Singapore's 277 square miles of dense urban landscape is not a policy failure. It is a physics and economics problem with no regulatory solution. T-Mobile leads the US market in 2026 by most metrics: 5G covers 98% of Americans, with more than 300 million people reached by mid-band coverage and over 210 million by the faster C-band frequencies. The company's layer-cake spectrum approach — 600 MHz low-band for geographic reach, 2.5 GHz mid-band for capacity, millimeter-wave in high-density urban areas — is widely cited as the most technically sophisticated 5G coverage strategy among major market operators. The FCC's C-band spectrum auctions raised more than $81 billion from operators eager to secure mid-band capacity. What T-Mobile, AT&T, and Verizon have not solved — and cannot solve through investment alone — is rural America. The economics of building and operating base stations in areas where each site serves dozens rather than thousands of users are marginal even with favorable regulatory treatment. The US operating environment score of 0.639 reflects genuinely favorable conditions: commercially flexible spectrum policy, no net neutrality bar on network slicing, multiple competing national carriers driving technology investment. The consumer outcomes score of 0.460 reflects what happens when the best operating environment in the Western world meets continental-scale geography. Australia: Operating Environment's Limits in Practice Australia's score pattern mirrors the United States — fifth on operating environment, seventh on consumer outcomes — but compresses into an even starker geographic fact: Australia is the world's sixth-largest country by land area, with 85% of its 26 million people concentrated in about 1% of its territory along the southeastern and southwestern coastal fringe. Telstra holds the Australian 5G Coverage Experience award from Opensignal for the fifth consecutive time as of October 2025, with a score of 7.6 out of 10 — three points ahead of second-placed Optus. In May 2026, Optus led the overall award table with six outright wins across speed and experience categories, while Vodafone Australia benefited from a network-sharing agreement with Optus that extended its geographic coverage to approximately one million square kilometers and population coverage to 98.4%. That deal — structurally similar to VodafoneThree's MOCN deployment in the UK — demonstrates how network sharing can solve coverage gaps that no single operator could close economically alone. Australia's operating environment is genuinely strong: energy costs are lower than the UK's, planning processes are more streamlined, and the three-operator market structure (Telstra, Optus, Vodafone) is consolidated enough to sustain infrastructure investment without the margin erosion of a fragmented MVNO market. The consumer outcomes gap is not a policy failure but a geography tax — the cost of connecting a population that is simultaneously concentrated and spread across a continent. France and Spain: Past Infrastructure as Present Insulation The most counterintuitive result in the index is France: ninth on operating environment and fourth on consumer outcomes, a five-position upward jump that sits in apparent contradiction. Spain shows a similar pattern, climbing from tenth to sixth. France's consumer outcomes are sustained by prior investment. All four French MNOs — Orange, SFR, Free, and Bouygues — cover more than 99% of the French population on 4G. Orange has ranked first in the French regulator ARCEP's quality-of-service assessments for 15 consecutive years. The dense network built during years of competitive 4G deployment continues to deliver acceptable consumer experience even as the current operating environment, depressed by price competition and MVNO margin pressure, makes fresh capital investment harder to justify. The mechanism is straightforward: price competition at the consumer level pushed French operators to densify their networks to retain subscribers, and that densification continues to serve users. What the operating environment scores reflect is that this dynamic is self-limiting — at some point, the margins required to sustain maintenance and upgrade investment no longer exist, and network quality begins to erode. France and Spain are currently living on infrastructure credit. The MMI's implicit argument is that they are approaching the limit of what past investment can sustain without a change in the investment environment. Hungary: Good Environment, Worst Outcomes Hungary presents the MMI's most troubling divergence. It sits seventh on operating environment — ahead of the United Kingdom, France, and Spain — and last on consumer outcomes at 0.410. The Hungarian mobile market has structural strengths: 15-year spectrum license terms give operators long investment runways, and 5G peak speeds in Budapest have exceeded 500 Mbps in testing. Magyar Telekom reached 86% outdoor 5G population coverage by end-2025, increasing the number of mobile cells by one-fifth during the year. Yettel (owned by Czech PPF Group) holds the country's fastest network title per the Hungarian regulator NMHH's March 2025 measurements, with a Speed Score of 137.26 against Magyar Telekom's 60.51 and One Hungary's 40.4. But Hungary also charges the highest average monthly price for unlimited 5G data in Europe. The combination of high consumer prices and last-place consumer outcomes suggests a market that has captured the conditions for investment but is not translating them into quality. 5G Standalone deployment remains opaque — Yettel announced SA in November 2023 without specifics, and neither Magyar Telekom nor One Hungary has publicly confirmed SA deployment across their consumer base. Hungary's EU funds (SZIP and RRF mechanisms) are supporting expansion, but the gap between operating environment score and consumer outcomes points to something structural: investment conditions are necessary but not sufficient when regulatory accountability for quality is weak. Photograph: Peter Turnley/Getty Images View image in fullscreen A soldier in Red Square, Moscow, during the attempted coup in 1991. Photograph: Peter Turnley/Getty Images Book of the day History books Review The August Coup by Robert Service review – the drink-soaked collapse of the Soviet Union This brilliant account of attempts by the old guard to take back control captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully John Simpson Mon 3 Aug 2026 02.00 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google M arxist-Leninist rule in Russia lasted 74 years, and in August 1991 it effectively collapsed in just three days: clear evidence of how hollowed out it had become. In the period that followed, Russia tried parliamentary democracy and unalloyed capitalism, then sank back into autocracy. Now it’s struggling under a wholly unnecessary war against its neighbour and former possession, Ukraine. Why did the system of Lenin, Stalin, Khrushchev and Brezhnev vanish so fast, without a fight? Because that’s how regimes fall in Russia: look at tsarism in 1917. (It almost happened again in June 2023, when the warlord Yevgeny Prigozhin’s men marched on Moscow largely unopposed; Vladimir Putin might have gone the way of Nicholas II had he not made some pretty wholesale promises to Prigozhin, then allegedly blown him up two months later.) Mikhail Gorbachev came to power in 1985 with the intention of saving the USSR. Instead, he oversaw its death. He was a charming, decent man but no visionary, and the two medicines he brought to the patient’s bedside, perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness), proved to be wholly ineffective. The brief coup of August 1991 against him, headed by Vladimir Kryuchkov, the boss of the KGB, was the kneejerk response of a bureaucracy that knew things were going wrong but had absolutely no idea what to do about it. It failed quickly, and Gorbachev was back at his desk within days, but the coup had damaged him fatally. Four months later, at the end of 1991, he was bundled out of power by the tough, brutal, boozy muzhik, Boris Yeltsin. Robert Service, author of The August Coup , is the English-speaking world’s foremost historian of 20th-century Russia and Bolshevism. His biographies of the three major Soviet leaders, Lenin, Stalin and Trotsky, are outstanding, even in that crowded field. In writing about the death of the system that these prodigies and monsters helped to create, Service has displayed a remarkable grasp of the vast sources, and a delightfully clear writing style which makes even the complexities of Soviet bureaucracy easy to understand. Compared with his earlier subjects, the story of the coup against Gorbachev and the collapse of the USSR is moderately simple; but Service guides the reader through the chaos of the collapsing system and the machinations of the coup leaders with ease and grace. The acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire day After the fall of the Berlin Wall in November 1989 and the loss of the various Soviet satrapies in eastern and central Europe , the USSR was falling apart, and Gorbachev, as its president, was shedding power and influence. No one knew how many Soviet republics would break away, and Gorbachev’s plan for running the rump of the union was bitterly contested. Yeltsin was the president of the Russian Republic, the largest, richest and most effective part of the old USSR. The two men were in angry contention. The coup leaders didn’t support either of them: they wanted to go back to a system which would restore as much Soviet power as possible. The assumption at the time was that the KGB had led the coup to protect its own interests, but Service demonstrates that Kryuchkov, the KGB boss, was much more concerned about the overall collapse of the Soviet system. And anyway, many KGB officers refused to join the coup. I was lucky enough to be in Moscow during those extraordinary days. Service captures the ludicrousness of it all beautifully. The coup leaders lost their faith in what they were doing almost immediately, and many of them didn’t have much to begin with. They argued, betrayed each other, or were paralysed by fear or torpor. Most of the people involved left some account of what happened, so the records available to Service were particularly rich. He provides us with a graphic description of the fatal press conference that the plotters gave at 5pm on the first day of the coup. The acting president, Gennady Yanayev, was supposedly in charge, but he had been drinking solidly for an entire day and his hands were visibly shaking. The press conference was broadcast live on state television, so everyone could see the condition he was in. After that, failure was certain. The basic reason it collapsed, though, was that the plotters didn’t manage to get hold of Yeltsin. It was easy enough to imprison Gorbachev at his palatial residence, Zarya, on the Crimean coast, where he was holidaying with his wife Raisa and their daughter; but Yeltsin remained free, and had use of the Russian republic’s Moscow headquarters, known as the White House. You might expect communist plotters to be good at cutting communications and taking over the media, but no one stopped Yeltsin from phoning allies and friends around Russia and across the world. Nor did they try to prevent him making his famous speech from a tank in front of the White House, condemning the coup and pledging to support democracy. It was a good speech, and the television coverage of it was seen worldwide. Again, no one pulled the plugs. Journalists like me were able to broadcast live throughout the coup. Yeltsin stayed inside the White House, mostly protected by a small crowd of unarmed demonstrators whose numbers dropped as the first night wore on and the rain came down. Yet Yeltsin suffered from the same weaknesses as many of the plotters. In the lobby of the White House I begged to be allowed to go up to his office and interview him, but was told he was too busy speaking to world leaders and organising the opposition. Later, the former Soviet foreign minister Eduard Shevardnadze arrived to see him. When he came out of the building an hour afterwards, he announced that Yeltsin had told him he would defend Russia’s freedom to the last drop of blood in his body. Stirring stuff. Three years later I reminisced with Shevardnadze about it all. He laughed. “When I got into Yeltsin’s office, he was lying unconscious on the floor with a couple of empty vodka bottles beside him.” But what about him fighting to his last drop of blood? “What do you think would have happened if I’d come out and told you I couldn’t speak to Yeltsin because he was dead drunk?” Such was the chaos and absurdity surrounding the death of the Soviet Union. In the days that followed no one had any idea where authority lay. The famously brave and entrepreneurial cameraman Rory Peck and I marched into KGB headquarters, the Lubyanka, and filmed in Kryuchkov’s own office. After that we even filmed among the ultra-secret KGB files. The next day Rory offered to buy the contents of the Central Museum of the Revolution for a million dollars. Only the fact that the official in charge couldn’t find a bank prepared to accept that much cash stopped the deal going through. We tend to forget the details of this pivotal episode. Perhaps Russia’s troubled history since 1991 has wiped them from our memories. Now Service has brought his magnificent grasp of Soviet history to the task of chronicling the ludicrous way it ended: not with a bang, but with the clink of vodka bottles. Bartlomiej Kubkowski on Sunday became the first person to swim across the Baltic Sea from Sweden to Poland, which was a nearly 100-mile quest. Kubkowski began the journey on Friday in Kaseberga, Sweden and finished in Dziwnow, Poland, capping off a nonstop swim that took more than 55 hours to complete. It was Kubkowski’s fifth attempt at completing the swim. Last year, in his fourth try, he was pulled unconscious from the water roughly seven miles from the finishing point. In addition to Kubkowski, Polish swimmer Karolina Szczepaniak attempted to become the first woman to finish the swim, but she was pulled from the water about 25 miles from the finish. Kubkowski didn’t sleep during the entire journey and was given food and water on a pole by an accompanying boat, which he wasn’t allowed to touch at any point. He had to arrive on the beach under his own power and stand without assistance for the swim to be official, according to reports. Kubkowski managed to do so, but was obviously exhausted at the end. View this post on Instagram The swim served as a fundraiser for “Cancer Fighters,” an organization that helps fund research and treatments for childhood cancer. https://monacolife.net/monaco-among-firs.text: Monaco among first to sign Council of Europe treaty to seize criminal assets by: Cassandra Tanti 15/10/2026 Follow Follow Follow Like Monaco was one of just eight countries to sign a new Council of Europe treaty in Strasbourg on Wednesday that will make it easier to trace, freeze and confiscate the proceeds of crime, including crypto-assets, as the Principality works to strengthen its credentials in the fight against financial crime. Monaco signed alongside Georgia, Greece, Hungary, Luxembourg, Montenegro, San Marino and the United Kingdom, as well as the European Union, making it one of the first of the Council of Europe’s 46 member states to back the agreement. The treaty was opened for signature on 14th October during the Council of Europe’s annual Octopus conference on cybercrime. Closing in on criminal money The treaty is an Additional Protocol to the 2005 Warsaw Convention, the Council of Europe’s main instrument against money laundering and terrorist financing. It is designed to modernise asset recovery in the face of criminal networks that are increasingly sophisticated, transnational and technologically advanced. Under the new rules, courts will be able to confiscate property linked to wider criminal conduct, in some cases without a criminal conviction, and target assets held by third parties, while protecting those who acquired them in good faith. Authorities will also be able to freeze or seize assets urgently, without prior notice, before they can be moved or hidden. Signatory states will be required to set up dedicated offices to trace and manage criminal assets, respond to requests from their counterparts within set deadlines, including within three days in urgent cases, and give financial intelligence units better access to financial and virtual-asset data. “Criminal money sustains organised crime. It also buys what should never be for sale: our democracies. Taking that money away is democratic security,” said Council of Europe Secretary General Alain Berset. “No state can recover criminal assets across borders on its own. With this protocol, none will have to.” Where the money goes Confiscated assets will be returned first to victims or their rightful owners. Sums above €10,000 will, as a rule, be shared equally between the countries involved in recovering them, and states are encouraged to put confiscated assets to social or public use. The protocol will enter into force once it has been ratified by five states, at least three of them Council of Europe members. A theme of Monaco’s presidency For Monaco, the signature carries particular weight. The Principality has held the rotating presidency of the Council of Europe’s Committee of Ministers since May, a term that runs until November, and has placed the fight against financial crime at the centre of it. In June, Monaco’s presidency led a declaration adopted by justice ministers from all 46 member states committing them to strengthen the identification, freezing and recovery of criminal proceeds, including crypto-assets. At the time, Monaco’s Secretary of State for Justice, Samuel Vuelta Simon, described the fight against money laundering and terrorist financing as “a long-term political commitment”. The signature also comes as Monaco works to leave the grey list of the Financial Action Task Force (FATF), the global anti-money laundering watchdog, which placed the Principality under increased monitoring in June 2024. In June this year, the FATF concluded that Monaco had substantially completed the action plan agreed at that time, clearing the way for an on-site visit by assessors, one of the final steps before removal. The Additional Protocol was adopted by the foreign ministers of the Council of Europe’s 46 member states at their annual session in Chișinău on 15th May 2026.
